title: Oryza sativa
wiki_lead:
Oryza sativa, having the common name Asian cultivated rice, is the much more common of the two rice species cultivated as a cereal, the other species being O. glaberrima, African rice. It was first domesticated in the Yangtze River basin in China 13,500 to 8,200 years ago.
Oryza sativa belongs to the genus Oryza and the BOP clade in the grass family Poaceae. With a genome consisting of 430 Mbp across 12 chromosomes, it is renowned for being easy to genetically modify and is a model organism for the study of the biology of cereals and monocots.
wiki_fulltext:
Oryza sativa, having the common name Asian cultivated rice, is the much more common of the two rice species cultivated as a cereal, the other species being O. glaberrima, African rice. It was first domesticated in the Yangtze River basin in China 13,500 to 8,200 years ago.
Oryza sativa belongs to the genus Oryza and the BOP clade in the grass family Poaceae. With a genome consisting of 430 Mbp across 12 chromosomes, it is renowned for being easy to genetically modify and is a model organism for the study of the biology of cereals and monocots.


Description

O. sativa has an erect stalk stem that grows 80–120 cm (30–45 in) tall, with a smooth surface. The leaf is lanceolate, 15–30 cm (5+7⁄8–11+3⁄4 in) long, and grows from a ligule 10–20 mm (3⁄8–3⁄4 in) long.


Taxonomy

Oryza sativa contains two major subspecies: the sticky, short-grained japonica or sinica variety, and the nonsticky, long-grained indica rice variety. Japonica was domesticated in the Yangtze Valley 6,000–9,000 years ago, and its varieties can be cultivated in dry fields (it is cultivated mainly submerged in Japan), in temperate East Asia, upland areas of Southeast Asia, and high elevations in South Asia, while indica was domesticated around the Ganges 4,500–8,500 years ago, and its varieties are mainly lowland rices, grown mostly submerged, throughout tropical Asia. Rice grain occurs in a variety of colors, including white, brown, black (purple when cooked), and red.
A third subspecies, which is broad-grained and thrives under tropical conditions, was identified based on morphology and initially called javanica, but is now known as tropical japonica. Examples of this variety include the medium-grain 'Tinawon' and 'Unoy' cultivars, which are grown in the high-elevation rice terraces of the Central Cordillera Mountains of northern Luzon, Philippines.
Glaszmann (1987) used isozymes to sort O. sativa into six groups: japonica, aromatic, indica, aus, rayada, and ashina.
Garris et al. (2004) used simple sequence repeats to sort O. sativa into five groups: temperate japonica, tropical japonica and aromatic comprise the japonica varieties, while indica and aus comprise the indica varieties. The Garris scheme has held up against newer analyses as of 2019, though one 2014 article argues that rayada is distinct enough to be its own group under japonica.


Etymology
The generic name Oryza is derived from the Ancient Greek word for rice, while the specific epithet sativa means "cultivated".


Genetics


Mapping and research tools
An accurate and usable simple sequence repeat marker set was developed and used to generate a high-density map.
A multiplex high-throughput marker assisted selection system has been developed but as with other crop HTMAS systems has proven difficult to customize, costly (both directly and for the equipment), and inflexible.
Other molecular breeding tools have produced rice blast resistant cultivars. DNA microarray has been used to advance understanding of hybrid vigor in rice, QTL sequencing has been used to elucidate seedling vigor, and genome wide association study (GWAS) by whole genome sequencing (WGS) has been used to investigate various agronomic traits.
In total, 641 copy number variations are known. Exome capture often reveals new single nucleotide polymorphisms in rice, due to its large genome and high degree of DNA repetition.


Specific genes
SPL14/LOC4345998 is a gene that regulates the overall architecture/growth habit of the plant. Some of its epialleles increase rice yield. \
Resistance to the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe grisea is provided by various resistance genes including Pi1, Pi54, and Pita. O. sativa uses the plant hormones abscisic acid and salicylic acid to regulate immune responses. Salicylic acid broadly stimulates, and abscisic acid suppresses, immunity to M. grisea; success depends on the balance between their levels.
O. sativa has a large number of insect resistance genes specifically for the brown planthopper. As of 2022, 15 R genes have been cloned and characterized.
Several O. sativa accessions also contain genetic adaptations to flooding. The Submergence 1 (Sub1) locus on chromosome 9 includes Sub1A, an ethylene-response-factor-like gene; the tolerance-specific Sub1A-1 allele is a major determinant of survival under complete submergence. In deepwater rice, the ethylene-response-factor genes SNORKEL1 and SNORKEL2 promote rapid internode elongation, allowing plants to adapt to rising floodwater.
grok_lead: Oryza sativa, commonly known as Asian rice or simply rice, is a semi-aquatic annual grass species in the Poaceae family that ranks as one of the world's most important staple crops, providing essential calories and nutrition to over half of the global population, particularly in Asia where it accounts for about 90% of total production. Native to tropical and subtropical regions of Asia, it was domesticated from wild progenitors such as Oryza rufipogon approximately 8,000 to 13,000 years ago, marking one of the earliest instances of plant cultivation in human history. As a monocotyledonous plant, O. sativa features fibrous roots, hollow stems (culms) that can grow 0.5 to 2 meters tall, and narrow, linear leaves with a rolled ligule; its inflorescence is a panicle bearing spikelets that develop into grains after self-pollination. The species is distinguished from the African cultivated rice ( Oryza glaberrima) by its adaptation to diverse ecosystems, including flooded paddies and upland fields, and it thrives in warm, humid climates with temperatures between 20â37Â°C and annual rainfall exceeding 1,000 mm. Oryza sativa encompasses two primary subspecies â indica and japonica âwhich diverged during domestication and exhibit distinct morphological, physiological, and geographic traits. Indica varieties, predominant in tropical lowlands of South and Southeast Asia, are characterized by longer, slender grains, greater tillering, and sensitivity to photoperiod, making them suitable for irrigated or rainfed systems. In contrast, japonica varieties, including temperate and tropical types, feature shorter, rounder grains, stronger culms, and better cold tolerance, and are mainly cultivated in higher latitudes such as East Asia, parts of Europe, and upland areas. Over 40,000 varieties exist worldwide, reflecting extensive breeding for traits like yield, disease resistance, and grain quality, with ongoing genetic research enhancing resilience to abiotic stresses like drought and salinity. Globally, rice production exceeds 500 million metric tons annually, supporting food security for billions while facing challenges from climate change, water scarcity, and pests; major producers include China, India, and Indonesia, which together account for over 60% of output. Cultivation typically involves transplanting seedlings into flooded fields to suppress weeds and optimize nutrient uptake, though direct-seeded and upland methods are also used in water-limited regions. Beyond its role as a primary carbohydrate sourceâcontributing up to 50% of caloric intake in many Asian dietsârice provides vitamins, minerals, and proteins, and serves industrial purposes in products like rice bran oil and starch.
